key: The Hamsa homed in light, the Vasu in mid-air, the priest beside the altar, in the house the guest, Dweller in noblest place, mid men, in truth, in sky, born of flood, kine, truth, mountain, he is holy Law.
s: Closing a hymn to the steed Dadhikravan, the verse names one being by his many dwellings; Sāyaṇa, on 4.40.5, reads them as the Sun, wind and fire, and the Sun as one with the Self in every creature and with the unconditioned Brahman.
src: Sāyaṇa, Vedārthaprakāśa on Rig Veda 4.40.5, sa.wikisource (printed edition not named), revision 216198 (2019)

evidence.words: अनया सौर्यर्चा य एषोऽन्तरादित्ये हिरण्मयः पुरुषो दृश्यते हिरण्यश्मश्रुः' (छा. उ. १.६. ६) इत्यादिश्रुत्युक्तो मण्डलाभिमानी देवोऽस्ति यश्च सर्वप्राणिचित्तरूपस्थितः परमात्मा यच्च निरस्तसमस्तौपाधिकं परं ब्रह्म तत्सर्वमेकमेवेति प्रतिपाद्यते ॥ "हंसः । हन्तिर्गत्यर्थः । सर्वत्र सर्वदा गन्ता ‘ योऽहं सोऽसौ' इत्यादिश्रुत्युक्तप्रकारेणैकीकृत्योपास्यः परमात्ममन्त्रप्रतिपाद्य आदित्यः। स च शुचौ दीप्ते द्युलोके सीदतीति “शुचिषत् । अथ यदतः परो दिवो ज्योतिर्दीप्यते ' ( छा. उ. ३. १३. ७) इत्यादिश्रुतेः । अनेन द्युस्थानः आदित्यः प्रतिपादितः । स एव मध्यस्थानो वायुरित्याह । "वसुः सर्वस्य वासयिता वायुः । स च "अन्तरिक्षसत् अन्तरिक्षसंचारी । अथ तस्यैव क्षितिस्थानवैदिकाग्निरूपतामाह ।
evidence.gloss: By this verse to the Sun it is taught that the god presiding over the solar orb, the golden person seen within the sun of which scripture speaks (Chāndogya 1.6.6), the supreme Self abiding as the mind of every creature, and the supreme Brahman from which every limiting adjunct is removed, are all one. Haṃsa, from han, to go: the Āditya, going everywhere always, to be worshipped as one with the supreme Self; he sits in the bright heaven, so śuciṣat. By this the Sun whose seat is heaven is set forth; he says the same one is the wind whose seat is the mid-air: Vasu, the wind that makes all dwell, moving in the mid-air. Then he states that the same one takes the form of the Vedic fire whose seat is the earth.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 4.40.5, at [335,5]). Sāyaṇa opens his comment on 4.40.5 by saying the verse to the Sun teaches that the god of the solar orb, the supreme Self abiding as the mind of all creatures, and the Brahman free of every adjunct are one; he then takes haṃsa/śuciṣat as the Sun in heaven, vasu/antarikṣasat as the same one as wind, hotā/vediṣat and atithi as the same one as fire, nṛṣat as the supreme Self, and ṛtam as Brahman. The sentence carries exactly that. Wilson note 2 reports the same identification of the sun with Parabrahma. Plain sense faithful: the hymn is Dadhikrāvan’s (Sāyaṇa’s introduction: dādhikram, the last verse to Sūrya) and 4.40.5 is its last verse; no four words of the key verse repeated. Revision 216198 dated 2019-10-28 by the Wikisource API. entry-check ok.
